title: Who bought what
prompt: Marketing wants to thank customers for the products they bought. Write `solve(orders, order_items, products)` so it returns each customer and product pair once, with the product's name.
rules: A customer bought a product if one of the customer's orders has a line with that `product_id`. Each pair appears once, however many lines or orders it comes from.
The product list sometimes repeats a product row; repeated rows are exact copies. A product that isn't in the list keeps a missing `name`.
A line whose order isn't in `orders` is left out. An order with a missing `customer_id` gives pairs with a missing `customer_id`.
hints: Lines know the product, orders know the customer: join `order_items` to `orders` on `order_id`, then to `products` on `product_id`.
A customer who bought the same product on two lines now has two identical rows. Select the three columns and keep each row once.
Use a left join to `products` so a product missing from the list still counts. Join on `product_id` only: the line's `unit_price` is the price on the day, not today's.
explanation: Join lines to their orders for the customer, then to products for the name: `order_items.join(orders, on="order_id").join(products, on="product_id", how="left")`. Every line gives a row, so a customer who bought a product twice has repeated rows, and a repeated product row doubles them again. Here the question really is about distinct pairs, so `select("customer_id", "product_id", "name").distinct()` at the end is right; removing the product copies first with `products.dropDuplicates()` is good practice too. Joining on `["product_id", "unit_price"]` looks tidy but loses the name whenever the price has changed since the order.
